summary: Proceed. This is a sound, rules-clean extension of the landed single-program align to bs>32. One run can be read from the per-shape top_kernels rows: 4 rows removed, 1 new row added, and the code at bs<=32 is byte-identical, so those shapes act as a drift control. The real risk is that a serial two-pass loop in one CTA at n=2048 ends up as slow as the ~11.5 us it replaces.
justification: The profile of the current best (bc56182a80444d16) confirms the target rows exactly. At bs=128: index_elementwise 3.2, unrolled_elementwise (sorted_ids fill) 2.8, moe_align_block_size_kernel 2.7 and count_and_sort 1.8 us, 10.5 us in all. At bs=256: 3.3 + 2.8 + 2.8 + 2.6 = 11.5 us. Against 333/470 us, a full win is ~2-2.5% per shape and a realistic win is 1.5-2%, ~0.5% on the headline: inside one run's CI, as the spec admits. TASK.md gives every load equal weight, so 2 of the 6 loads moving ~1.5-2% is consistent with the expected directions. bs=1/8/16/32 are correctly predicted flat, because they keep _align_small. Weakest link: the new kernel's own time. The landed _align_small scales with n: 1.6 us (n=8), 2.7 (n=64), 2.9 (n=128), 4.4 (n=256, 4 warps, one [256,32] tile with cumsum). Extrapolating, the per-route cost is ~1-1.5 us per 128 routes, which mostly comes from the onehot cumsum/rank in pass 2. The chunked kernel at n=1024 (bs=128) and n=2048 (bs=256, 4 chunks of 512) runs pass 1 plus pass 2 serially in one CTA, with a loop-carried base[] dependency. 8 warps roughly halves the per-element cost, but a plausible range is ~5-8 us at bs=128 and ~8-14 us at bs=256. bs=128 should gain. bs=256 could come out flat or even slightly slower. The speed-of-light framing does not apply: this is launch and latency work, far from any bandwidth floor. Minor: the graph-node gap saved by removing 3 launches is only ~0.3-1 us in total (LESSONS).
confounders: marlin-block-m-two-smaller-on-postnorm: sets BSM=16 at bs=128 and BSM=32 at bs=256/257, which fixes cap (1504 / 3040), the padding-slot count and n_blocks (94 / 95). The chunked kernel's padding, cap-fill and block loops therefore cost what they cost at those BSMs. At SGLang's 48/64 the padding loops would be ~3x larger. This shifts the new kernel's own time somewhat, but not what Marlin receives, so it does not confound attribution of the align rows.

triton-map-align-on-block-m-restack / triton-map-align-small-m-port: same area and same kernel design. They gate on ALIGN_FUSED_MAX_TOKENS=32, so the bs>32 path this hypothesis replaces was never touched by them. They are the in-run control (bs<=32 code unchanged), not a confounder.

post-expert-norm-triton-small-m: no confound at the target shapes. bs>=32 still uses SGLang's fused_post_expert_norm_weighted_sum with slot_expert_ids=local_ids, which needs remote slots to be exactly -1. The new kernel must reproduce that, as _align_small does.
sglang-marlin-path-parity: the base pipeline. The 32-expert align capacity (M*8 + 32*(bsm-1)) that the chunked kernel must match comes from it. No interaction beyond that.
interference: No companion is warranted. Attribution needs no A/B: the change is visible directly in top_kernels at bs=128/256 (the four at::native/align rows disappear and _align_chunked_kernel appears with its own time). The four bs<=32 shapes are byte-identical code and serve as the drift reference. Reverting block-m-two-smaller (ab-revert) would only change BSM, which changes the kernel's padding-loop cost by about a microsecond and none of Marlin's work. It cannot flip the interpretation, and spending a check on it would be wasted with moe at 4 checks left. A CHUNK/num_warps ab-tune is a follow-up, not a companion: if the kernel row shows bs=128 winning and bs=256 losing, the next step is a gate at n<=1024 or a CHUNK=256 / 2-CTA variant, chosen from this run's rows. Read the result per shape: success means kernel row < ~(sum of removed rows - 1 us) at each verify shape. The headline is expected to stay inside the CI either way.
rules_flags: None blocking. The branch is on shape only (num_tokens > 32 and expert_map is not None). Nothing derived from inputs is cached. There are no host syncs in kernel_fn: n, cap and n_blocks are host ints from shapes, and allocations are shape-sized. Compilation and the self-check (.tolist/.item/synchronize) run in prepare(), untimed, on synthetic ids. That is fine.

Correctness hazard (not a rule, but it would fail the tests): pass 2 must recompute local ids from topk_ids (read-only) rather than reload local_ids_ptr written in pass 1. A load of global memory stored by other threads of the same CTA is not ordered without tl.debug_barrier(). The same goes for any reload of counts staged through memory. Keep counts/base/seg_start in registers.

The bs=257 and skewed-128 tests must pass: the skewed case puts most routes on a few experts, so one expert can get hundreds of routes in one chunk. The rank must be base[e] + within-chunk exclusive cumsum. The extended self-check over tokens (33, 128, 256, 257) with the skewed/all-one-expert/all-local patterns covers this. Make sure it is actually run at BSM 16 and 32, the picks at >=128, as well as at SGLang's picks for 33.
open_questions: What is the new kernel's own time at bs=256 (n=2048, 4 serial chunks x 2 passes)? If it exceeds ~10 us, the bs=256 gain disappears. Would CHUNK=256 with num_warps=8 (lower register pressure for the [CHUNK,32] int32 onehot and cumsum: 512x32 = 16K elements, 64 per thread at 8 warps), or recomputing the onehot only in pass 2, be faster?

Is unrolled_elementwise (2.8 us) really the wrapper's sorted_ids fill and not some other cast? topk_ids is already int32, so .to(int32) is a no-op. If it were something else that stays, the saving is smaller.

If the swap-AB rewrite later needs BSM=64/128 from this kernel, the [NUM_E, BSM] padding tile grows to 4K int32. That is fine for one CTA, but add those BSMs to the prepare compile list and the self-check, as the spec notes.
